bib.title: Do Language Models Need Sleep? Offline Recurrence for Improved Online Inference

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 15 pages, 55,163 chars. Body ends p.11 and refs run p.12-15. There is no appendix. Figures were not viewed, only their extracted captions and axis numbers.

TITLE: "Do Language Models Need Sleep? Offline Recurrence for Improved Online Inference" (footnote on p.3 says an earlier title was "Language Models Need Sleep").
AUTHORS: Sangyun Lee (Carnegie Mellon University, corresponding author), Sean McLeish (University of Maryland), Tom Goldstein (University of Maryland), Giulia Fanti (Carnegie Mellon University).
VENUE: preprint, arXiv:2605.26099v3 [cs.CL], 5 Jun 2026.

MAIN CLAIM: Before the KV cache is evicted, a hybrid SSM-attention model runs N offline recurrent passes ("sleep") over the accumulated context. These passes update the fast weights in its SSM blocks, and the model is trained end to end through the whole process. Answers are then produced in a single forward pass with no wake-time looping. More sleep passes help most on problems that need deeper sequential reasoning over context that has already been evicted. The authors argue the bottleneck is the compute spent turning context into weights, not memory capacity.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Rule 110 cellular automaton, t=32 rollout steps. Model: 4-layer GDN-attention hybrid, d=256. Context is hard-evicted every L=24 tokens. Train budget about 5B tokens.
   - No loop: "reaching only about 10% exact accuracy".
   - Two loops: about 20%.
   - Three and four loops: above 30%.
   - Setup caveats: the Muon learning rate was tuned on the N=1 baseline, and seeds and data order were fixed. The paper does not state seed counts or variance.
2. GSM-Infinite, Jet-Nemotron 2B (hybrid), window L=2000, problems of 2,000-3,300 tokens, 1,600 held-out examples, no chain-of-thought. Loops in the 1/2/4/6 sweep; baseline is N=1 (no loop).
   - Accuracy with 6 loops vs no loop: 0.742 to 0.812 on 6-operation problems, and 0.351 to 0.388 on 8-operation problems.
   - Easy 2- and 4-operation problems are near saturation (0.98-0.995) at any loop count.
3. GSM-Infinite, Ouro 1.4B plus 6 inserted Jet layers (under 10% more parameters), same setup. Accuracy with 4 loops vs no loop: 0.419 to 0.615 on 6-operation problems, and 0.210 to 0.272 on 8-operation problems.
4. GSM-Infinite with sliding-window eviction, Ouro 1.4B, L=512 (sequence is about 4-6x the window). Accuracy on 2-operation problems rises from 0.596 (N=1) to 0.905 (N=4), which the paper calls a 52% improvement. Other operation counts improve less (e.g. 0.251 to 0.320 on 6-operation). The sliding-window runs use a warm-up of one epoch on the Jet layers, then two epochs of full training.
Also: on Depo (k-hop graph retrieval, 10-layer d=512 model trained from scratch, window L=75, total length 360), the 1-loop model stalls at 4 hops and beyond, 2 loops stall at 8 hops and beyond, and only 4 loops begin to improve on 16 hops (p.8). No accuracy numbers are given for Depo, only test-loss curves.

QUOTES
- p.1 (abstract): "a model periodically converts recent context into persistent fast weights before clearing its key-value cache. During the sleep, the model performs N offline recurrent passes over the accumulated context and updates the fast weights in its state-space model (SSM) blocks through a learned local rule."
- p.2: "the bottleneck is not merely memory capacity as suggested by prior work [32, 2], but the amount of computation available for transforming evicted context into a useful internal state."
- p.11 on cost: "during training, we need to perform N deeper forward and backward passes, which can make training slow and unstable."

LIMITS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT SHOW
- The method needs fast-weight SSM blocks (GDN or Jet) inside a hybrid model. The weights consolidated are the SSM recurrent state, trained with a learned rule. This is not gradient-based test-time training and not context distillation into the parametric MLP weights. For the note's "parametric memory" section, "fast weights" here means a recurrent state matrix, not LoRA or fine-tuning.
- It is trained and evaluated only on synthetic tasks (Rule 110, Depo, GSM-Infinite), and the authors call the models "modest-scale pretrained models" (Broader Impact). It does not test real long-context agent workloads, general web text, or frontier-scale models.
- Training cost grows roughly linearly with N (Fig. 6b), and training is sequential across windows. The authors concede instability and slowness. Sleep also adds a pause with no input, so the benefit is lower wake-time latency, not lower total compute.
- Failure claims are made "under a fixed training-token budget", not in principle.
- The paper says nothing about forgetting, interference between successive consolidations, or multi-session persistence. It gives no comparison against RAG, summarization or compaction. It does not test a standard transformer, because under hard eviction one is at chance by construction.
- No variance or seed counts are reported. Some gains are small (0.351 to 0.388).

BUILDS ON
- Fast weights and linear recurrence: Schmidhuber-style fast weights, Mamba2 (Dao and Gu, 2024), Gated Delta Networks (Yang et al., 2025), Hybrid models (Arora et al., 2024, arXiv:2402.18668).
- Depth-recurrent and looped models: Geiping et al., Ouro (Zhu et al., arXiv:2510.25741, 2025), McLeish et al. [39] for the Muon recipe.
- Test-time training with sliding-window attention: Tandon et al. [55], who take one gradient step per chunk.
- Context distillation: Askell et al. 2021, Caccia et al. 2025.
- Cartridges / self-study: Eyuboglu et al.
- Offline planning and sleep: Lin et al. [35], Momennejad et al. [42], Behrouz et al. [6].
- Tasks: Allen-Zhu, "Physics of LMs 4.1" (NeurIPS 2025), GSM-Infinite (Zhou et al., ICML 2025 workshop).
- Years for the unnamed references come from the reference list, which I did not fully check. Check the reference list before citing them.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Fig. 1 (p.6) is a schematic. It shows the ATTN/SSM stack looped x N at the eviction boundary, with the KV cache discarded and the fast weights kept. It is the clearest picture of "consolidate context into weights". Fig. 4 (p.10) is the best results figure. It shows accuracy against operation count for each loop count, and the gap widens at 6 and 8 operations.

PROBLEMS: none significant. The PDF contained no embedded instructions. The figures' axis text was extracted as noise but is consistent with the captions.
